chapter_sections.label: DEFINITION:
chapter_sections.text:
Light is a form of energy that makes objects visible to our eyes. We see objects
because light emitted by or reflected from those objects enters our eyes.

chapter_sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Objects that emit their own light are called LUMINOUS OBJECTS (e.g., Sun, fire, electric lamp).
Objects that are seen due to reflected light are called ILLUMINATED OBJECTS (e.g., Moon, furniture).
Light travels in a straight line.
Light is reflected from all surfaces.
Splitting of white light into its constituent colours is called DISPERSION.
The human eye has several parts: cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina and optic nerve.
Visually impaired persons can read and write using the BRAILLE SYSTEM.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
Things become visible when light emitted by or reflected from them enters our eyes.
Objects that produce their own light are luminous objects; objects seen by reflected
light are illuminated objects.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: We see objects only when light from them enters our eyes.
Light may be emitted by the object itself (luminous) or reflected by it (illuminated).
LUMINOUS OBJECTS: Sun, stars, fire, electric lamp, candle flame -- they emit their own light.
ILLUMINATED OBJECTS: Moon, furniture, book, walls -- they reflect light from other sources.
In complete darkness, no objects can be seen because no light enters the eyes.
Light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation).

sections.label: ACTIVITY 13.1: (Activity on Reflection)
sections.aim: To observe reflection of light using a comb and mirror.
sections.materials:
White sheet of paper, drawing board, comb, black paper strip,
torch, plane mirror strip.
procedure: 1. Fix a white sheet of paper on a drawing board or table.
2. Take a comb and close all openings except one in the middle using black paper.
3. Hold the comb perpendicular to the sheet of paper.
4. Throw light from a torch through the middle opening of the comb.
5. A narrow ray of light will be seen on the paper on the other side of the comb.
6. Place a plane mirror strip in the path of this light ray.
sections.observation: After striking the mirror, the ray of light is reflected in another direction.
sections.conclusion:
Light is reflected by a mirror. The light ray hitting the surface is
called the INCIDENT RAY. The ray coming back after reflection is the REFLECTED RAY.

DIAGRAM:
[Fig. 13.1 -- Arrangement for showing reflection: torch sending ray through comb,
ray hitting mirror, reflected ray shown on paper.]

EXERCISE 13.1.1: Suppose you are in a dark room. Can you see objects in the room?
Can you see objects outside the room? Explain.
EXERCISE ANSWER: In a dark room, we cannot see any objects because there is no light
to reflect from objects and enter our eyes. We cannot see objects outside the
room either because no light from outside enters through the closed room.
Vision requires light to enter our eyes from objects.

items.question: What are luminous objects? Give two examples.
items.answer:
Objects that produce their own light are called luminous objects.
Examples: Sun, electric lamp (any two).

items.question: Define illuminated objects with an example.
items.answer:
Objects that are visible because they reflect light from luminous objects are
called illuminated objects. Example: Moon, book (any one).

items.question: Explain how we see objects in our surroundings.
items.answer:
We see objects only when light from them enters our eyes.
Step 1: Light from a luminous source (like the Sun or a lamp) falls on an object.
Step 2: The object reflects some of this light in all directions.
Step 3: When this reflected light enters our eyes, we see the object.
In a dark room without any light source, we cannot see any object.

items.question: Differentiate between luminous and non-luminous (illuminated) objects.
items.answer:
Luminous Objects:
- Produce their own light.
- Can be seen even in absence of external light source.
- Examples: Sun, fire, electric lamp.
Non-luminous (Illuminated) Objects:
- Do not produce own light; reflect light from other sources.
- Cannot be seen without an external light source.
- Examples: Moon, chair, book.

items.question: Describe the activity to show that light travels in a straight line
items.answer:
Materials: Drawing board, white paper, comb, black paper, torch, plane mirror.
Procedure:
1. Fix white paper on the drawing board.
2. Cover all openings of a comb with black paper except the middle one.
3. Hold the comb perpendicular to the paper and shine a torch through the opening.
4. A narrow ray of light is seen traveling in a straight line on the paper.
5. Place a plane mirror in the path of the ray.
Observation: The ray hits the mirror and returns in a different direction as the reflected ray.
Conclusion: Light travels straight and is reflected by smooth surfaces.

items.question: What are the conditions necessary for us to see an object?
items.answer:
Two conditions are necessary to see an object:
Condition 1 -- There must be a source of light. Without light, no object can be seen.
Condition 2 -- Light from the object (emitted or reflected) must enter our eyes.
Additional factors: Our eyes must be open and functioning. The object must be
within the field of view. Even a luminous object cannot be seen if it is behind
a wall or opaque obstacle blocking the light path to our eyes.

items.question: Explain the difference between luminous and illuminated objects with
items.answer:
Luminous objects produce their own light. They emit light energy due to chemical
or nuclear reactions or electrical energy conversion. Examples: Sun (nuclear
fusion), electric lamp (electrical energy to light), candle (chemical energy).
Illuminated objects do not produce their own light. They are visible because
they reflect light coming from luminous objects. Examples: Moon, planets, furniture.
The Moon is an illuminated object. It receives light from the Sun and reflects
a part of it toward the Earth. When this reflected light reaches our eyes, we
see the Moon. The same principle applies to all planets and most objects around us.
Therefore, almost everything we see (except luminous sources) is seen due to
reflected light.

items.question: Which of the following is a luminous object?
items.explanation: Electric lamp produces its own light and is luminous. Moon, mirror, and book only reflect light; they are illuminated objects.

items.question: We can see objects in a room because --

options.B: light from objects enters our eyes

items.explanation: Vision occurs when light from an object (emitted or reflected) enters our eyes. Eyes receive light; they do not produce it.

items.question: Which of the following is an illuminated object?
items.explanation: Moon reflects sunlight and is an illuminated object. Sun, fire, and candle produce their own light and are luminous objects.

items.question: In a completely dark room with no light source, you will --

options.D: not see any objects at all

items.explanation: In complete darkness, no light is available. Without light entering the eyes, nothing is visible -- not even luminous objects (if the room is truly dark with no light source).

items.question: The light ray that falls on a reflecting surface is called --
items.explanation: The ray falling on the surface is the incident ray. The ray coming back after reflection is the reflected ray. Normal is perpendicular to the surface.

items.question: A ray of light appears as a narrow beam when passed through a single opening of a comb because --

options.B: light travels in a straight line

items.explanation: Light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation), so it passes straight through the opening without bending, forming a narrow beam.

items.question: Which of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.A: Luminous objects can only be seen in dark conditions.
options.B: Illuminated objects produce their own light.
options.C: Almost all objects we see daily are illuminated objects.
options.D: The Sun is an illuminated object because it is very bright.

items.explanation: Almost everything around us (furniture, books, walls) reflects light and is illuminated. The Sun itself is luminous but most everyday objects are illuminated. Illuminated objects do NOT produce their own light.

items.question: When a narrow beam of light from a torch passes through one opening of a comb, the light seen on the other side will be --

options.A: a wide beam spreading in all directions
options.C: a curved beam following the comb shape
options.D: no beam, as comb blocks all light

items.explanation: Since light travels in a straight line, it passes through the narrow opening and continues straight, forming a narrow beam on the other side.

items.question: The concept of "seeing" involves which sequence?

options.A: Light source -- Eyes emit light -- Object reflects -- We see
options.B: Light source -- Object reflects light -- Light enters eyes -- We see
options.C: Object emits sound -- Eyes detect -- We see
options.D: Eyes produce light -- Hits object -- Returns -- We see

items.explanation: Correct sequence: light from a source hits the object, the object reflects light, reflected light enters our eyes, we see the object. Eyes never emit light; they only receive it.

items.question: Which object among these can be seen even if there is absolutely no external light source in the surroundings?
items.explanation: A glowing tube light (luminous object) produces its own light and can be seen even in darkness. Mirror, white paper, and Moon are illuminated objects that need external light to be visible.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
Reflection is the bouncing back of light when it strikes a surface. The laws
governing this reflection are called the Laws of Reflection.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: INCIDENT RAY: The ray of light that falls on the reflecting surface.
REFLECTED RAY: The ray of light that bounces back after reflection.
NORMAL: A line drawn perpendicular to the reflecting surface at the point where
the incident ray meets the surface.
ANGLE OF INCIDENCE (angle i): The angle between the incident ray and the normal.
ANGLE OF REFLECTION (angle r): The angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
LAW 1: The angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection (angle i = angle r).
LAW 2: The incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence and the reflected
ray all lie in the same plane.
These laws hold for all reflecting surfaces, smooth or rough.
A ray of light thrown along the normal reflects back along the same path
(because angle of incidence = 0, so angle of reflection = 0).
PROPERTIES OF IMAGE IN A PLANE MIRROR:
The image is VIRTUAL (cannot be obtained on a screen).
The image is ERECT (upright, not upside down).
The image is of the SAME SIZE as the object.
The image is as far BEHIND the mirror as the object is in FRONT of it.
The image undergoes LATERAL INVERSION (left appears as right and right as left).
LATERAL INVERSION: In the image formed by a plane mirror, the left side of the
object appears as the right side in the image and vice versa. This is called
lateral inversion.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 13.1 (Detailed verification of both laws of reflection):
sections.aim: To verify the first law of reflection and measure angles of incidence and reflection.
sections.materials: Drawing board, white paper, comb (with one opening), black paper, torch, plane mirror.
procedure: 1. Fix white sheet on drawing board.
2. Cover all comb openings except one with black paper.
3. Hold comb at one end, shine torch through the open slit.
4. A narrow ray appears on the paper; mark its path.
5. Place mirror in the path; mark the reflected ray.
6. Draw a normal at the point where the incident ray meets the mirror.
7. Measure the angle of incidence (between incident ray and normal).
8. Measure the angle of reflection (between reflected ray and normal).
9. Repeat by changing the angle of incidence several times.
10. Record readings in Table 13.1 (5 rows).
sections.observation: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection in every trial.
sections.conclusion:
Angle of incidence = Angle of reflection (First Law of Reflection).

sections.label: ACTIVITY 13.2:
sections.aim: To verify the second law of reflection (coplanarity of incident ray, normal, reflected ray).
sections.materials: Stiff paper (chart paper), torch with comb (one opening), plane mirror.
procedure: 1. Repeat Activity 13.1 with chart paper projecting beyond edge of table.
2. Allow the reflected ray to fall on the projecting portion of paper.
3. Bend the projecting portion of paper downward (creating a different plane).
sections.observation: The reflected ray can no longer be seen on the bent portion.
sections.conclusion:
Incident ray, normal and reflected ray must all lie in the same plane.
When the paper is bent, they are no longer coplanar, so the reflected ray is not visible.

EXERCISE 13.2.1: State the laws of reflection.
EXERCISE ANSWER:
Law 1: The angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection.
Law 2: The incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence and the reflected
ray all lie in the same plane.

EXERCISE 13.2.2: Describe an activity to show that the incident ray, the reflected
ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane.
EXERCISE ANSWER:
Activity: Fix a white sheet of paper on a drawing board. Place a comb against
a stiff paper or chart paper projecting beyond the edge of a table. Throw light
from a torch through the comb. A reflected ray appears on the paper. The whole
sheet of paper (representing one plane) contains the incident ray, the normal
and the reflected ray. When the projecting portion of the sheet is bent, the
reflected ray cannot be seen anymore, showing all three must lie in the same plane.

sections.label: EXERCISE 13.2.3: Fill in the blanks:
sections.raw:
(a) A person 1 m in front of a plane mirror seems to be 2 m away from his image.
(b) If you touch your LEFT ear with right hand in front of a plane mirror, it will
be seen in the mirror that your right ear is touched with LEFT HAND.
EXERCISE ANSWER: (a) 2 m  (b) left hand

EXERCISE 13.2.4 (MCQ): Angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.
(a) Always  (b) Sometimes  (c) Under special conditions  (d) Never
EXERCISE ANSWER: (a) Always

EXERCISE 13.2.5 (MCQ): Image formed by a plane mirror is --
(a) virtual, behind the mirror and enlarged.
(b) virtual, behind the mirror and of the same size as the object.
(c) real at the surface of the mirror and enlarged.
(d) real, behind the mirror and of the same size as the object.
EXERCISE ANSWER: (b) virtual, behind the mirror and of the same size as the object.

EXERCISE 13.2.6: What is the angle of incidence of a ray if the reflected ray is
at an angle of 90 degrees to the incident ray?
EXERCISE ANSWER: If the reflected ray is at 90 degrees to the incident ray, and since
angle of incidence = angle of reflection, let each angle = x.
Then x + x = 90 degrees, so 2x = 90 degrees, therefore x = 45 degrees.
The angle of incidence is 45 degrees.

EXERCISE 13.2.7: Two mirrors meet at right angles. A ray of light is incident on
one at an angle of 30 degrees (Fig. 13.19). Draw the reflected ray from the second mirror.
EXERCISE ANSWER: Angle of incidence on first mirror = 30 degrees.
Angle of reflection from first mirror = 30 degrees (law of reflection).
Angle of incidence on second mirror = 90 - 30 = 60 degrees (geometry of right angle).
Angle of reflection from second mirror = 60 degrees.
The final reflected ray is parallel to the original incident ray (property of two
mirrors at right angles).

EXERCISE 13.2.8: Boojho stands at A just on the side of a plane mirror (Fig. 13.20).
Can he see himself in the mirror? Also can he see the image of objects at P, Q and R?
EXERCISE ANSWER: Boojho at A (just on the side/edge of the mirror) will NOT be able to
see himself because the incident ray from him does not hit the mirror. He can see
the image of object at P (near the mirror face) but NOT the images of Q and R
which are too far to the side for the reflection to reach his eyes at A.

EXERCISE 13.2.9: (a) Find the position of the image of object at A in plane mirror
(Fig. 13.21). (b) Can Paheli at B see this image? (c) Can Boojho at C see this
image? (d) When Paheli moves from B to C, where does the image of A move?
EXERCISE ANSWER:
(a) The image of A is formed as far behind the mirror as A is in front of it,
directly opposite A.
(b) Yes, Paheli at B can see the image of A if she is within the field of view.
(c) Yes, Boojho at C can also see the image of A if C is within the field of view.
(d) The image of A does NOT move when Paheli moves from B to C. The image stays
fixed at its position behind the mirror; only the observer's position changes.

items.question: State the two laws of reflection.
items.answer:
Law 1: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.
Law 2: The incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence and the reflected
ray all lie in the same plane.

items.question: Define angle of incidence and angle of reflection.
items.answer:
ANGLE OF INCIDENCE: The angle between the incident ray and the normal drawn
at the point of incidence on the reflecting surface.
ANGLE OF REFLECTION: The angle between the reflected ray and the normal drawn
at the point of incidence on the reflecting surface.

items.question: What is lateral inversion? Give an example from daily life.
items.answer:
When an object is placed in front of a plane mirror, its image appears such
that the left side of the object appears as the right side in the image and the
right side appears as the left side. This phenomenon is called lateral inversion.
Example: When we raise our right hand in front of a mirror, the image appears
to raise its left hand. Similarly, text appears reversed (left-right) in a mirror.

items.question: What are the characteristics of an image formed by a plane mirror?
items.answer:
1. The image is virtual (cannot be obtained on a screen).
2. The image is erect (same orientation as the object).
3. The image is of the same size as the object.
4. The image is formed as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
5. The image undergoes lateral inversion (left and right are interchanged).

items.question: Describe the activity to verify the first law of reflection.
items.answer:
Activity to verify angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
Materials: Drawing board, white paper, comb (one opening), torch, plane mirror.
Procedure:
1. Fix white paper on drawing board. Cover all comb slits except one with black paper.
2. Shine torch through the open slit to get a narrow ray on the paper.
3. Place plane mirror in the path of the ray.
4. Mark the incident ray, the point of incidence and the reflected ray.
5. Draw the normal at the point of incidence.
6. Measure angle of incidence (angle i) and angle of reflection (angle r).
7. Repeat with different angles.
Observation: In every trial, angle i = angle r.
Conclusion: First law of reflection is verified.

items.question: A person stands 2 m in front of a plane mirror. Where is his image
items.answer:
The image is formed 2 m behind the mirror (same distance as the object is
in front). The person and his image are thus 4 m apart (2 m in front + 2 m behind).
Properties of the image:
1. Virtual: The image cannot be captured on a screen.
2. Erect: The image is upright.
3. Same size: The image is the same height as the person.
4. Laterally inverted: Left and right sides are interchanged.

items.question: Explain the two laws of reflection with the help of a diagram.
items.answer:
Laws of Reflection:
The two laws of reflection are:
Law 1: The angle of incidence (angle i) is always equal to the angle of reflection (angle r).
Law 2: The incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence and the reflected
ray all lie in the same plane.

Diagram: [A horizontal line representing mirror surface; a perpendicular line
(normal) at the midpoint; incident ray coming from upper left making angle i with
normal; reflected ray going to upper right making angle r with normal; angle i = angle r]

Experiment to verify Law 1:
Materials: Drawing board, white paper, comb (one opening), torch, plane mirror.
Steps: Shine narrow beam on mirror using comb. Mark incident ray, reflected ray,
and draw normal. Measure angle i and angle r. Repeat with 4 more angles. In all
trials, angle i = angle r. Law 1 verified.

Experiment to verify Law 2:
Use chart paper projecting beyond table. Mark incident and reflected rays. All
three (incident ray, normal, reflected ray) lie on the flat sheet (one plane).
Bend the projecting paper to a different plane -- the reflected ray is no longer
visible there, proving it stays in the original plane. Law 2 verified.

items.question: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. This is --
items.explanation: "Angle of incidence = angle of reflection" is the first law of reflection. The second law states that incident ray, normal and reflected ray are coplanar.

items.question: The normal is --

options.B: a line perpendicular to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence
options.D: a line parallel to the mirror surface

items.explanation: The normal is drawn perpendicular (90 degrees) to the mirror surface at the exact point where the incident ray hits the surface.

items.question: An image formed in a plane mirror is --
items.explanation: The image in a plane mirror is virtual (cannot be obtained on screen) and erect (upright), same size as the object and laterally inverted.

items.question: A ray of light is incident on a plane mirror at an angle of 35 degrees. What is the angle of reflection?
items.explanation: By the first law of reflection, angle of incidence = angle of reflection. So the angle of reflection = 35 degrees.

items.question: If a ray of light is incident along the normal to a mirror, what happens to the reflected ray?

options.A: It returns along the same path
options.B: It goes perpendicular to the incident ray
options.C: It is absorbed by the mirror
options.D: It bends away from the normal

items.explanation: If the incident ray is along the normal, the angle of incidence = 0. Therefore angle of reflection = 0, meaning the reflected ray returns along the same path as the incident ray.

items.question: LATERAL INVERSION means --

options.A: the image is upside down compared to the object
options.B: the left and right sides of the image are interchanged
options.C: the image is smaller than the object
options.D: the image is larger than the object

items.explanation: Lateral inversion is the interchange of left and right sides in the mirror image. The image is erect (not upside down) and the same size as the object.

items.question: A person stands 3 m in front of a plane mirror. The distance between the person and his image is --
items.explanation: Image is formed 3 m behind the mirror. Person is 3 m in front. Total distance between person and image = 3 + 3 = 6 m.

items.question: A ray of light is reflected from a plane mirror. The angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray is 80 degrees. The angle of incidence is --
items.explanation: The angle between incident and reflected ray = angle i + angle r = 80 degrees. Since angle i = angle r, we get 2 x angle i = 80, so angle i = 40 degrees.

items.question: Which law of reflection states that the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane?
items.explanation: The second law of reflection states that incident ray, normal at point of incidence and reflected ray are coplanar (lie in the same plane).

items.question: Activity 13.2 proves the second law of reflection by bending the chart paper. What is observed when the paper is bent?

options.A: The reflected ray is seen on the bent portion
options.B: The reflected ray disappears because the paper is now in a different plane

items.explanation: When the paper is bent, the reflected ray is no longer in the same plane as the incident ray. Since the second law requires coplanarity, the reflected ray cannot be seen on the bent portion, confirming the second law.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
When parallel rays of light fall on a surface and are reflected as parallel rays,
it is called REGULAR (or SPECULAR) REFLECTION. When reflected rays go in different
directions, it is called DIFFUSED (or IRREGULAR) REFLECTION.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: REGULAR REFLECTION: Occurs on smooth, polished surfaces (mirror, calm water).
All parallel incident rays are reflected as parallel rays. An image is formed.
DIFFUSED REFLECTION: Occurs on rough or irregular surfaces (cardboard, paper, wall).
Parallel incident rays are reflected in many different directions. No image is formed.
Both types of reflection obey the laws of reflection at every point.
Diffused reflection is caused by irregularities in the surface, not failure of laws.
Most objects around us are visible due to diffused reflection.
Images are formed only by regular reflection.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 13.4:
sections.aim:
To understand that parallel rays incident on an irregular surface reflect in
different directions (diffused reflection).
sections.materials: Imaginary irregular surface (as described in Fig. 13.6).
procedure: Imagine parallel rays falling on an irregular surface. Apply the laws
of reflection at each point. The normals at different points on the rough surface
point in different directions, so reflected rays go in different directions.
sections.observation: Reflected rays are NOT parallel; they go in various directions (Fig. 13.7).
sections.conclusion:
An irregular surface causes diffused reflection. The laws of reflection
still hold at each individual point of the surface.

DIAGRAMS:
[Fig. 13.6 -- Parallel rays incident on an irregular surface: incoming parallel arrows
hitting a jagged surface with normals at different angles]
[Fig. 13.7 -- Rays reflected from irregular surface in different directions]
[Fig. 13.8 -- Regular reflection: parallel rays reflecting from smooth mirror surface,
all reflected rays parallel]

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS:
sections.text:
- A cinema screen is designed to give diffused reflection so that the image can be
seen from all positions in the hall.
- A mirror gives regular reflection, forming sharp images.
- The same object may give regular reflection from one part (polished) and diffused
reflection from another (rough) part.

EXERCISE 13.3.1: Differentiate between regular and diffused reflection. Does
diffused reflection mean the failure of the laws of reflection?
EXERCISE ANSWER:
Regular Reflection: Occurs when light falls on a smooth, polished surface
(like a mirror). Reflected rays are parallel and an image is formed.
Diffused Reflection: Occurs when light falls on a rough or irregular surface
(like cardboard). Reflected rays go in different directions and no image is formed.
No, diffused reflection does NOT mean failure of the laws of reflection. The
laws of reflection hold at every point of the rough surface, but because the
surface is uneven, the normals at different points point in different directions,
causing reflected rays to scatter.

EXERCISE 13.3.2: Mention against each of the following whether regular or diffused
reflection will take place when a beam of light strikes. Justify your answer in each case.
EXERCISE ANSWER:
(a) Polished wooden table -- Regular reflection (smooth, polished surface)
(b) Chalk powder -- Diffused reflection (rough surface)
(c) Cardboard surface -- Diffused reflection (rough surface)
(d) Marble floor with water spread over it -- Regular reflection (smooth water layer)
(e) Mirror -- Regular reflection (smooth, polished surface)
(f) Piece of paper -- Diffused reflection (rough surface)

items.question: What is regular reflection?
items.answer:
When a parallel beam of light falls on a smooth, polished surface and the
reflected rays also form a parallel beam going in one direction, it is called
regular reflection. Images are formed by regular reflection.

items.question: What is diffused reflection? Does it mean the laws of reflection fail?
items.answer:
When a parallel beam of light falls on a rough or irregular surface and the
reflected rays scatter in all different directions, it is called diffused reflection.
No, the laws of reflection DO NOT fail. They are obeyed at every individual point;
but since the surface is uneven, the normals at each point point differently,
causing scattering of reflected rays.

items.question: Differentiate between regular and diffused reflection.
items.answer:
Regular Reflection:
- Occurs on smooth, polished surfaces (mirror, calm water).
- Reflected rays are parallel.
- An image is formed.
- Example: Reflection from a mirror or still water.
Diffused Reflection:
- Occurs on rough, irregular surfaces (cardboard, paper).
- Reflected rays go in different directions.
- No image is formed.
- Example: Reflection from a wall or rough cloth.

items.question: Why can we see the same object from many different directions?
items.answer:
We can see the same object from many different directions because most
objects have rough surfaces that cause diffused reflection. When light falls
on a rough surface, it is reflected in all directions. This means that
wherever we stand (from any direction), some reflected light reaches our eyes,
allowing us to see the object from multiple angles. Regular reflection (as from
a mirror) only reflects light in one direction and would not allow this.

items.question: You have polished wooden table, chalk powder, cardboard and a mirror.
items.answer:
Regular Reflection:
- Polished wooden table: smooth surface reflects parallel rays as parallel rays.
- Mirror: most polished surface; perfect regular reflection; image is formed.
Diffused Reflection:
- Chalk powder: extremely rough particles scatter light in all directions.
- Cardboard: rough surface with fibres causes scattered reflection.
Justification: Regular reflection requires smooth surface (parallel normals at all
points). Rough surfaces have normals pointing in different directions at each point,
so reflected rays scatter -- but the laws of reflection hold at each individual point.

items.question: Explain why a cinema screen gives a better view from all seats while
items.answer:
A cinema screen is made of a rough, white material that produces diffused
reflection. When light from the projector hits the screen, it is scattered in all
directions, so viewers sitting anywhere in the hall can see the image on the screen.
A mirror produces regular reflection -- reflected light goes in only one specific
direction. So only viewers in that specific direction can see the image, while
others cannot. Therefore, a cinema screen (diffused reflection) is better for
viewing from all seats compared to a mirror (regular reflection).

items.question: Explain regular and diffused reflection with neat diagrams.
items.answer:
Regular Reflection:
When parallel rays fall on a smooth, polished surface, all normals at the points
of incidence are parallel (perpendicular to the smooth surface). By the law of
reflection (angle i = angle r), each ray reflects at equal angle, producing
reflected rays that are parallel. This forms a clear image. Examples: Mirror,
calm water.
[Diagram: Parallel incoming arrows hitting smooth flat surface, parallel normals,
parallel reflected arrows going out]

Diffused Reflection:
When parallel rays fall on a rough, uneven surface, the normals at different
points of incidence point in different directions (because the surface is tilted
differently at each point). Each ray obeys the law of reflection (angle i = angle r
at its own point), but since normals differ, each ray reflects in a different
direction. The reflected rays scatter in all directions. No image is formed.
Examples: Paper, cardboard, wall.
[Diagram: Parallel incoming arrows hitting jagged surface with normals in all
directions, reflected arrows going in different directions]

Why not failure of laws:
At EACH individual point of the rough surface, the angle of incidence equals the
angle of reflection. The laws of reflection hold precisely. It is only because the
surface irregularities cause the normals to tilt differently at each point that
the reflected rays scatter. The scattering is due to surface geometry, not any
violation of the laws.

items.question: Regular reflection takes place when light falls on --
items.explanation: Regular reflection requires smooth, polished surfaces where all normals are parallel. Rough surfaces cause diffused reflection.

items.question: In diffused reflection, reflected rays --

options.A: are all parallel to each other

items.explanation: In diffused reflection, surface irregularities cause normals to point in different directions, so reflected rays scatter in all directions.

items.question: Which surface gives regular reflection?
items.explanation: A plane mirror has a smooth, polished surface that causes regular reflection. Cardboard, rough wall, and paper are rough and cause diffused reflection.

items.question: Why does a cinema screen give diffused reflection?

options.A: It is made of a very smooth surface
options.B: It is made of a rough surface that scatters light in all directions

items.explanation: A cinema screen has a rough white surface. When projector light hits it, diffused reflection scatters light in all directions, so viewers at any angle can see the image.

items.question: Diffused reflection is caused by --

options.A: failure of the laws of reflection

items.explanation: Diffused reflection occurs because a rough surface has normals pointing in different directions at each point, causing each reflected ray to go in a different direction. Laws of reflection hold at every point.

items.question: When parallel rays fall on an irregular surface, they --

options.C: are reflected in various different directions
options.D: pass through the surface without reflection

items.explanation: An irregular surface has uneven normals; each point reflects light at its own angle. The result is reflected rays going in different (scattered) directions.

items.question: You look at yourself in a mirror and in a white rough wall. In which case do you see a clear image and why?

options.A: Rough wall -- because diffused reflection reaches your eyes from all directions
options.B: Mirror -- because regular reflection forms a clear image

items.explanation: A mirror (regular reflection) forms a clear virtual image. A rough wall (diffused reflection) scatters light in all directions so no image is formed, only a diffuse glow.

items.question: In which of the following situations do the laws of reflection NOT apply?

options.A: When light hits a rough surface
options.B: When light hits a smooth surface
options.C: When light hits a coloured surface
options.D: The laws of reflection apply in all situations

items.explanation: The laws of reflection apply universally to all surfaces. Even in diffused reflection from rough surfaces, each individual point obeys the laws. There is no situation where the laws of reflection do not apply.

items.question: The key difference between regular and diffused reflection is --

options.A: the colour of the light used
options.B: the smoothness or roughness of the reflecting surface
options.C: the angle at which light falls
options.D: whether the light is from a natural or artificial source

items.explanation: Regular reflection occurs from smooth surfaces (mirror), diffused reflection from rough surfaces. The nature of the surface determines the type of reflection, not the angle or source of light.

items.question: A book is visible from all directions in a well-lit room. This is because --

options.A: the book emits its own light
options.B: the book absorbs all light and re-emits it
options.C: the rough surface of the book causes diffused reflection in all directions
options.D: the book undergoes regular reflection from its polished surface

items.explanation: A book has a rough paper surface. Diffused reflection scatters light from the book's surface in all directions, allowing it to be seen from any angle. This is the same reason most objects around us are visible from multiple positions.

topics.topic_name: REFLECTED LIGHT CAN BE REFLECTED AGAIN

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
Light reflected from one surface can fall on another surface and be reflected again.
This multiple reflection allows objects to be seen around corners using devices like
the periscope.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Reflected light obeys the same laws of reflection when it hits another surface.
A PERISCOPE uses two plane mirrors to allow viewing of objects not directly visible.
Periscopes are used in submarines, tanks and by soldiers in bunkers.
The principle: Mirror 1 reflects light to Mirror 2; Mirror 2 reflects it to the eye.
Can the reflected rays be further reflected? Yes -- reflected light is still light
and can be reflected again by any surface.
PERISCOPE:
Two plane mirrors are fixed at 45 degrees to the vertical inside a long tube.
Light from the object hits Mirror 1 (at 45 degrees) and reflects downward.
This reflected light hits Mirror 2 (at 45 degrees) and reflects horizontally
into the observer's eye.
The observer can see objects above or around obstacles.
Used in: Submarines (to see above water surface), tanks, military bunkers,
and by spectators to see over crowds.
DIAGRAM:
[Fig. 13.9 -- Mirror at hair dresser's shop: showing front mirror, back mirror,
and how reflected light from the back mirror shows the back of a person's head]
ACTIVITY (Observation -- Hair Dresser's Shop -- Multiple Reflection):
AIM: To understand that reflected light can be reflected again using two mirrors.
SETUP: Sit in front of a large plane mirror (Mirror 1). The hair dresser holds
a second mirror (Mirror 2) behind your head.
OBSERVATION: You can see the back of your head in Mirror 1.
ACTIVITY EXPLANATION: Light from the back of your head reflects off Mirror 2 (behind you),
then that reflected light falls on Mirror 1 (in front of you) and reflects again
into your eyes -- double reflection allows you to see the back of your head.
CONCLUSION: Reflected light obeys the same laws of reflection and can be reflected
again by another mirror. This is the principle of multiple reflection.

items.question: Can reflected light be reflected again? Give an example.
items.answer:
Yes, reflected light can be reflected again. Example: At a hair dresser's
shop, light from the back of the head is reflected by the mirror held behind,
then this reflected light is again reflected by the front mirror to reach the
person's eyes, allowing them to see the back of their own head.

items.question: What is a periscope and what is its principle?
items.answer:
A periscope is a device that uses two plane mirrors to enable viewing of
objects that are not in the direct line of sight. Its principle is multiple
reflection: light from an object is reflected by one mirror and this reflected
light is again reflected by a second mirror into the observer's eye.

items.question: Explain how a periscope works with the help of a diagram.
items.answer:
A periscope has two plane mirrors fixed at 45 degrees to the tube wall inside
a vertical tube, one at the top and one at the bottom.
Working:
Step 1: Light from the object (e.g., above water) hits the top mirror at 45 degrees.
Step 2: The top mirror reflects the light downward through the tube.
Step 3: This reflected light hits the bottom mirror (also at 45 degrees).
Step 4: The bottom mirror reflects the light horizontally to the observer's eye.
The observer can thus see objects that are above or around an obstacle.
[Diagram: Vertical tube with mirror at top-left (45 degrees) and mirror at bottom-right
(45 degrees); light path: horizontal -- mirror 1 -- vertical down -- mirror 2 -- horizontal to eye]

items.question: Where are periscopes used? Explain any one application in detail.
items.answer:
Periscopes are used in:
1. Submarines
2. Tanks
3. Military bunkers
4. Watching events over crowd
Submarine application: A submarine travels under water. To see what is happening
above the water surface, sailors use a periscope that extends above the water level.
Light from ships or coastlines enters the top mirror, reflects down the tube, hits
the bottom mirror and reflects into the submarine crew's eyes. This way they can
see above water while staying submerged.

items.question: Explain how you can see the back of your head using mirrors at a
items.answer:
At a hair dresser's shop, two mirrors are used:
- Mirror 1: A large plane mirror fixed on the wall in front of you.
- Mirror 2: A hand-held mirror held behind your head by the hair dresser.
Process:
1. Light from the back of your head falls on Mirror 2 (behind you).
2. Mirror 2 reflects this light toward Mirror 1 (in front of you).
3. Mirror 1 reflects this light into your eyes.
So you can see the back of your head in Mirror 1 through double reflection.
Principle: This illustrates that reflected light can be reflected again by another
mirror, and this multiple reflection can be used to see objects not in direct view.

items.question: How is a simple periscope constructed? Describe its construction and use.
items.answer:
Construction of a Simple Periscope:
Materials: A long cardboard tube or box (vertical), two plane mirrors.
Steps:
1. Take a long vertical cardboard tube.
2. Cut openings at the top and bottom on opposite sides.
3. Fix one plane mirror at 45 degrees to the tube at the top opening,
reflecting surface facing down.
4. Fix another plane mirror at 45 degrees to the tube at the bottom opening,
reflecting surface facing the top mirror.
5. The two mirrors face each other at 45 degrees.
Use: Hold the periscope vertically. Look through the bottom opening.
Light from above enters through the top opening, reflects off the top mirror
downward, reflects off the bottom mirror horizontally into your eyes.
This lets you see objects above an obstacle (wall, crowd, waterline) while
remaining hidden below.

items.question: Explain the principle of multiple reflection with examples.
items.answer:
Principle of Multiple Reflection:
When light is reflected from a surface, the reflected light is still light
obeying all properties of light, including the ability to be reflected again
from another surface. This is called multiple reflection. Each reflection
follows the laws of reflection.
Example 1: Hair dresser's shop -- double reflection (back mirror + front mirror)
allows you to see the back of your head.
Example 2: Kaleidoscope -- multiple reflections from three mirrors create
beautiful patterns.
Example 3: Periscope -- double reflection allows viewing around corners or
above obstacles.

Periscope -- Principle and Construction:
Principle: Uses double reflection. Two plane mirrors at 45 degrees reflect
light twice to redirect its path by 90 degrees at each mirror, resulting in
the final image being directly visible to the observer.
Construction:
- Long vertical tube (cardboard or metal).
- Top: plane mirror at 45 degrees facing inward-downward.
- Bottom: plane mirror at 45 degrees facing inward-upward.
- Openings cut at top (one side) and bottom (opposite side).
Working: Object's light enters top opening --> reflects off top mirror downward
--> travels down tube --> reflects off bottom mirror horizontally --> enters observer's eye.
Applications:
1. Submarines: Crew sees above water surface while submerged.
2. Military tanks and bunkers: Soldiers observe enemy without exposing themselves.
3. Medical endoscopes (advanced principle).
4. Watching events over a crowd -- observer stands behind crowd, periscope
shows what is happening in front.

items.question: A periscope works on the principle of --
items.explanation: A periscope uses two mirrors to reflect light twice (multiple reflection) to redirect the light path and allow seeing around obstacles.

items.question: In a periscope, each plane mirror is fixed at an angle of --
items.explanation: Each mirror is fixed at 45 degrees to the vertical. This causes light to reflect at 90 degrees (turning its path from horizontal to vertical and back to horizontal) through double reflection.

items.question: Periscopes are commonly used in --
items.explanation: Periscopes allow viewing above the water line for submarines or over walls for tanks and soldiers in bunkers.

items.question: At a hair dresser's shop, you can see the back of your head because --

options.B: light from the back of your head undergoes multiple reflection between two mirrors
options.C: the mirror behind you is a concave mirror
options.D: your eyes can see in all directions simultaneously

items.explanation: Light from the back of your head reflects off the mirror behind you, then that reflected light reflects off the front mirror to reach your eyes. This is double/multiple reflection.

items.question: Which of the following devices makes use of multiple reflection?
items.explanation: A periscope uses two plane mirrors to reflect light twice, changing its path so the observer can see around obstacles. The other devices do not use multiple reflection.

items.question: In a periscope, light from an object above a wall is first reflected by the top mirror. What does the second mirror do?

options.B: Reflects the light toward the observer's eye
options.C: Reflects the light back toward the object

items.explanation: The second mirror (at the bottom of the periscope) receives the light reflected downward by the top mirror and reflects it horizontally toward the observer's eye, completing the periscope action.

items.question: A soldier in a bunker wants to see enemy movements outside without exposing himself. The best device he should use is --
items.explanation: A periscope allows viewing objects in a different line of sight by using double reflection. The soldier can hold the periscope above the bunker edge while remaining hidden, using it to see outside.

items.question: If the two mirrors in a periscope are arranged parallel to each other (not at 45 degrees), the periscope will --

options.A: work better because parallel mirrors give infinite images
options.B: not function as a periscope because light will not be redirected properly

items.explanation: The 45-degree angle is essential for redirecting light by 90 degrees at each mirror. Parallel mirrors would not redirect the light path to reach the observer's eye; the periscope would not function properly.

items.question: Reflected light from Mirror 1 falls on Mirror 2. Which statement is TRUE about the reflection from Mirror 2?

options.A: The laws of reflection do not apply to reflected light
options.B: The reflected light from Mirror 1 acts as incident light on Mirror 2
options.C: Mirror 2 absorbs reflected light and does not reflect it
options.D: The reflected light cannot be reflected again by any surface

items.explanation: Reflected light is still light. When it falls on Mirror 2, it acts as incident light and undergoes reflection again following the same laws of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection).

items.question: The principle behind a submarine periscope allows the crew to see --

options.B: objects above the water surface while the submarine is submerged
options.C: objects through the metal hull of the submarine
options.D: objects that are very far away using magnification

items.explanation: The periscope tube extends above the water surface. Light from objects above water reflects through the tube via two mirrors at 45 degrees, allowing the submerged crew to see above the waterline.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
When two or more plane mirrors are placed at an angle to each other, an object
placed between them forms MORE THAN ONE IMAGE due to multiple reflections.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: A single plane mirror forms only ONE image of an object.
Two mirrors placed at an angle form MULTIPLE IMAGES due to repeated reflections
between the mirrors.
NUMBER OF IMAGES formed by two mirrors at angle theta:
Number of images = (360 / theta) - 1 (when 360/theta is a whole number)
At 90 degrees: images = (360/90) - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3 images.
At 60 degrees: images = (360/60) - 1 = 6 - 1 = 5 images.
At 45 degrees: images = (360/45) - 1 = 8 - 1 = 7 images.
At 120 degrees: images = (360/120) - 1 = 3 - 1 = 2 images.
Two PARALLEL mirrors (0 degrees or 180 degrees): INFINITE images.
This principle is used in a KALEIDOSCOPE to create beautiful patterns.
KALEIDOSCOPE:
Made of three rectangular mirror strips joined to form a prism (triangular cross-section).
Coloured pieces of glass are placed at one end; the other end has a peephole.
Multiple reflections create beautiful, symmetrical patterns.
No two patterns are ever the same.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 13.5:
sections.aim: To make a kaleidoscope and observe the patterns formed.
sections.materials:
Three rectangular mirror strips (each 15 cm x 4 cm), adhesive tape,
circular cardboard tube or thick chart paper tube, one cardboard disc with a hole
in the centre, one circular plane glass plate, one ground glass plate, small pieces
of coloured glass (broken bangles).
procedure: 1. Join the three mirror strips with adhesive tape to form a triangular prism
(mirrors facing inward).
2. Fix this prism arrangement inside a circular cardboard tube slightly longer
than the mirror strips.
3. Close one end of the tube with the cardboard disc having a hole in the centre
(peephole). Paste transparent plastic sheet under this disc to make it durable.
4. At the other end (touching the mirrors), fix the circular plane glass plate.
5. Place several small pieces of coloured glass on this glass plate.
6. Close this end with the ground glass plate to keep the coloured pieces inside.
sections.observation:
When you look through the hole and rotate the tube, you see beautiful
symmetrical coloured patterns that keep changing.
sections.conclusion:
Multiple reflections from three mirrors create beautiful patterns.
Each rotation gives a new, unique pattern. A kaleidoscope is based on the principle
of multiple images from multiple mirrors.

DIAGRAM:
[Fig. 13.10 -- Images in plane mirror at right angle: showing two mirrors meeting
at right angles with coin in between and 3 images visible]
[Fig. 13.11 -- Image in plane mirror parallel to each other: showing infinite
images of a candle between two parallel mirrors]
[Fig. 13.12 -- Making a kaleidoscope: (a) triangular prism of mirrors,
(b) tube fitted with peephole disc, (c) tube with coloured glass end]

EXERCISE 13.5.1: Describe the construction of a kaleidoscope.
EXERCISE ANSWER: Take three rectangular mirror strips each about 15 cm long and 4 cm wide.
Join them together to form a prism (triangular cross-section). Fix this arrangement
in a circular cardboard tube slightly longer than the mirror strips. Close one end
with a cardboard disc having a hole in the centre. At the other end, fix a circular
plane glass plate. Place small pieces of coloured glass (broken bangles) on this
glass plate. Close this end with a ground glass plate. When you look through the
hole and rotate the tube, beautiful patterns are seen due to multiple reflections.

EXERCISE 13.5.2: How many images of a candle will be formed if it is placed between
two parallel plane mirrors separated by 40 cm?
EXERCISE ANSWER: Infinite (unlimited) images are formed when an object is placed between
two parallel plane mirrors.

items.question: How many images are formed when an object is placed between two
items.answer:
When two plane mirrors are set at right angles (90 degrees), the number of
images formed = (360/90) - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3 images.

items.question: What happens to the number of images as the angle between two
items.answer:
As the angle between two plane mirrors decreases, the number of images formed
increases. When the angle is very small (mirrors almost parallel), the number of
images becomes very large. For perfectly parallel mirrors (angle = 0), infinite
images are formed.

items.question: What is a kaleidoscope? On what principle does it work?
items.answer:
A kaleidoscope is an optical instrument that produces beautiful, symmetrical
patterns using multiple reflections. It consists of three rectangular mirror strips
joined to form a triangular prism (mirrors facing inward), placed inside a tube
with coloured glass pieces at one end and a peephole at the other end.
Principle: It works on the principle of multiple images formed by mirrors placed
at angles to each other. Three mirrors placed at 60 degrees to each other form
multiple reflections of the coloured glass pieces, creating beautiful and ever-changing
symmetrical patterns.

items.question: Find the number of images formed when two mirrors are placed at
items.answer:
Formula: Number of images = (360/angle) - 1
(a) At 60 degrees: (360/60) - 1 = 6 - 1 = 5 images
(b) At 45 degrees: (360/45) - 1 = 8 - 1 = 7 images
(c) At 120 degrees: (360/120) - 1 = 3 - 1 = 2 images

items.question: Describe the activity to find the number of images formed by two
items.answer:
Activity: Multiple Images with Two Plane Mirrors
Materials: Two plane mirrors, adhesive tape (to hinge), a coin.
Procedure:
1. Hinge two plane mirrors along one edge using tape.
2. Set them at 90 degrees and place a coin between them. Count images -- 3 images.
3. Set them at 60 degrees. Count images -- 5 images.
4. Set them at 45 degrees. Count images -- 7 images.
5. Set them at 120 degrees. Count images -- 2 images.
6. Set them parallel (180 degrees or 0 degrees). Count images -- infinite images (candle example shows countless images stretching into distance).
Observation: As angle decreases, number of images increases.
Conclusion: Formula N = (360/angle) - 1. Parallel mirrors give infinite images.
Application: Kaleidoscope uses this principle with 3 mirrors at 60 degrees to
generate beautiful patterns.

items.question: How do you make a kaleidoscope? Describe its construction step by step.
items.answer:
Construction of a Kaleidoscope:
Materials: Three rectangular mirror strips (15 cm x 4 cm each), adhesive tape,
circular cardboard tube, cardboard disc with central hole, plane glass plate,
ground glass plate, coloured glass pieces (from broken bangles).
Steps:
1. Join three mirror strips with reflecting surfaces facing inward to form a prism
(equilateral triangle cross-section). Hold with adhesive tape.
2. Insert this mirror prism inside the circular cardboard tube.
The tube should be slightly longer than the mirror strips.
3. At one end, fix a cardboard disc with a small hole in the centre (peephole).
Paste transparent plastic sheet under this for durability.
4. At the other end (touching the mirrors), place a circular plane glass plate.
5. Place several small pieces of coloured glass on this plate.
6. Seal this end with a ground glass plate (so coloured pieces can move freely
but not fall out).
Use: Look through the hole and rotate -- beautiful patterns appear!

items.question: Explain the phenomenon of multiple images with the help of an experiment.
items.answer:
Phenomenon of Multiple Images:
When two plane mirrors are placed facing each other at an angle, light from an
object placed between them bounces back and forth repeatedly between the mirrors.
Each bounce creates a new image. This results in multiple images.
Number of images formed = (360/angle) - 1 (when 360/angle is a whole number).

Experiment with two mirrors at 90 degrees:
Materials: Two plane mirrors, adhesive tape, coin.
Steps: Hinge two mirrors at 90 degrees. Place a coin between them.
Observation: 3 images of the coin are visible.
Verification: N = (360/90) - 1 = 3. Confirmed.

Varying the angle:
At 60 degrees: 5 images.
At 45 degrees: 7 images.
Parallel mirrors: infinite images.
Conclusion: Smaller angle = more images; parallel mirrors = infinite images.

Kaleidoscope:
Construction: Three mirror strips (15 cm x 4 cm) joined as a triangular prism
(inward-facing), placed in a cardboard tube. One end has peephole disc, other
end has plane glass + coloured glass pieces + ground glass plate.
Working: Coloured pieces are reflected by the three mirrors. Each mirror reflects
the image of all other coloured pieces plus the images in other mirrors. Multiple
reflections from three mirrors at 60 degrees create beautiful symmetrical patterns.
Rotating the tube rearranges the coloured pieces, creating new patterns every time.
No two patterns are ever identical -- hence kaleidoscopes are used by designers
of wallpapers, fabrics and jewellery for creative inspiration.

items.question: The number of images formed when two plane mirrors are placed at 90 degrees to each other is --
A kaleidoscope uses --

options.C: three plane mirrors forming a triangular prism

items.explanation: A kaleidoscope uses three rectangular mirror strips joined to form a triangular prism with mirrors facing inward, creating multiple reflections of coloured glass pieces.

items.question: When two plane mirrors are placed parallel to each other, the number of images formed is --
items.explanation: Parallel mirrors (angle = 0 degrees or 180 degrees) cause light to bounce back and forth infinitely, forming infinite images.

items.question: The number of images formed by two mirrors at 60 degrees is --
As the angle between two mirrors is decreased, the number of images formed --
items.explanation: From the formula N = (360/angle) - 1, as angle decreases, 360/angle increases, so N increases. Smaller angle = more images.

items.question: In a kaleidoscope, beautiful patterns are formed due to --

options.A: dispersion of light through glass pieces
options.C: multiple reflections of coloured glass pieces in three mirrors
options.D: refraction of light through the tube

items.explanation: The three mirrors in a kaleidoscope create multiple reflections of the coloured glass pieces, forming beautiful symmetrical patterns that change as the tube is rotated.

items.question: Two mirrors are placed at 45 degrees. The number of images formed is --
A kaleidoscope produces an interesting feature: you will never see the same pattern again. This is because --

options.A: the mirrors change angle each time
options.B: the coloured glass pieces rearrange randomly each time the tube is rotated
options.C: each colour is absorbed differently each time
options.D: the tube length changes with rotation

items.explanation: When the tube is rotated, the coloured glass pieces fall into a new random arrangement. Since three mirrors create multiple reflections of this arrangement, each new arrangement gives a completely new pattern, and random arrangements are essentially never repeated.

items.question: Which of the following correctly explains why two parallel mirrors give infinite images?

options.A: They absorb no light so all light is preserved as infinite images
options.B: Light bounces back and forth between them indefinitely (theoretically),
options.C: Parallel mirrors magnify each image infinitely
options.D: Each mirror produces one image, so two mirrors produce two, and adding

items.explanation: Light bounces between parallel mirrors repeatedly. Each bounce creates an additional image, and theoretically this continues indefinitely, giving infinite images (in practice, images become dimmer with each reflection).

items.question: An object is placed between two mirrors at 120 degrees to each other. The number of images formed is --

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
Sunlight (white light) consists of seven colours. When white light passes through
a prism, it splits into its constituent colours -- this is called DISPERSION OF LIGHT.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Sunlight is referred to as WHITE LIGHT.
White light consists of SEVEN COLOURS: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red
(remembered as VIBGYOR).
DISPERSION: Splitting of white light into its constituent colours is called dispersion.
Dispersion occurs when white light passes through a prism (glass prism or water prism).
RAINBOW: A natural phenomenon showing dispersion. Water droplets in the atmosphere
act as tiny prisms and split sunlight into seven colours.
Dispersion also occurs when sunlight reflects off a mirror in water (as in Activity 13.7).
ACTIVITY 13.7: Dispersion of Sunlight Using Mirror in Water
AIM: To show that sunlight (white light) consists of several colours.
MATERIALS: A katori (bowl) filled with water, a plane mirror, a white sheet of paper
or white wall.
PROCEDURE:
1. Get a plane mirror of a suitable size.
2. Place the mirror in the bowl (katori) filled with water (Fig. 13.13).
3. Position the bowl near a window or in sunlight so that direct sunlight falls
on the mirror.
4. Adjust the position of the bowl so the reflected light from the mirror falls
on a white wall or white paper sheet.
OBSERVATION: The reflected light on the white wall shows multiple colours --
Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red (VIBGYOR).
CONCLUSION: Sunlight (white light) consists of seven colours. The mirror and water
together act as a prism. The different colours are bent (refracted) by different amounts
when passing through the water, splitting white light into its constituent colours.
This is called dispersion of light.
CONCLUSION NOTE: Rainbow is a natural dispersion phenomenon where water droplets
in the atmosphere split sunlight into seven colours.
DIAGRAM:
[Fig. 13.13 -- Dispersion of light: bowl of water with mirror at an angle inside,
sunlight hitting mirror, reflected light showing rainbow colours on white wall]

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS:
sections.text:
- The band of colours obtained on dispersion of white light is called SPECTRUM.
- ORDER of colours in spectrum: VIBGYOR (Violet at one end, Red at the other).
- The amount of bending (refraction) differs for each colour: Violet bends the most,
Red bends the least.
- A glass triangular prism also disperses white light into VIBGYOR spectrum.
- Isaac Newton was the first to demonstrate dispersion of white light using a prism.

items.question: What is dispersion of light?
items.answer:
The splitting of white light into its constituent seven colours when it passes
through a prism (glass or water) is called dispersion of light.

items.question: Name the seven colours of sunlight in order.
items.answer:
The seven colours of sunlight in order are:
Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red.
(Memory aid: VIBGYOR)

items.question: Describe the activity to show that sunlight consists of several colours.
items.answer:
Activity: Dispersion using mirror in water.
Materials: Bowl (katori), water, plane mirror, white paper/wall, sunlight.
Procedure:
1. Place a plane mirror in a bowl of water.
2. Position near a window so sunlight falls on the mirror.
3. Adjust so reflected light falls on a white wall.
Observation: Reflected light shows seven colours -- VIBGYOR (Violet to Red).
Conclusion: Sunlight (white light) consists of seven colours. The mirror and water
together act as a prism and cause dispersion.

items.question: What is a rainbow? How is it formed?
items.answer:
A rainbow is a natural arc of seven colours seen in the sky after rain when
sunlight is present. It is a natural example of dispersion of light.
Formation:
1. After rain, the sky is filled with tiny water droplets.
2. Sunlight enters these water droplets and is refracted (bent).
3. Inside the droplet, the light undergoes total internal reflection.
4. When leaving the droplet, it is refracted again.
5. The different colours (VIBGYOR) bend by different amounts and emerge separately.
6. The combined effect of millions of droplets creates the arc of seven colours.

items.question: Is sunlight white or coloured? How can you prove it?
items.answer:
Sunlight appears white but actually consists of SEVEN colours mixed together.
This can be proved by the following activity:
Proof through Dispersion Activity:
1. Place a plane mirror in a bowl of water.
2. Let sunlight fall on the mirror.
3. Direct the reflected light onto a white wall.
Result: Seven colours (VIBGYOR) appear on the white wall.
This proves that sunlight (white light) contains all seven colours. When the water
acts as a prism, it separates the mixed colours by bending each colour by a different
amount (refraction). The separated colours appear as individual bands on the wall.
Natural Proof: A rainbow after rain shows the same seven colours -- proving that
sunlight consists of seven colours, separated by water droplets acting as prisms.

items.question: What is the spectrum of white light? Name the colours and state
items.answer:
The band of seven colours produced when white light (sunlight) is dispersed by
a prism is called the SPECTRUM of white light.
The seven colours in order (VIBGYOR):
1. Violet
2. Indigo
3. Blue
4. Green
5. Yellow
6. Orange
7. Red
Bending during Dispersion:
- VIOLET bends the MOST during dispersion (highest refraction).
- RED bends the LEAST during dispersion (lowest refraction).
- The other colours (Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange) bend by intermediate amounts.
This difference in bending causes the colours to separate, forming the spectrum.

items.question: Explain what sunlight consists of and describe two ways to prove it.
items.answer:
Nature of Sunlight:
Sunlight appears white to our eyes but is actually a mixture of seven colours:
Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red (VIBGYOR). When these seven
colours are mixed together in the right proportions, they produce white light.

Proof 1 -- Mirror in Water Activity:
Place a plane mirror in a bowl of water. Let sunlight fall on the mirror at an angle.
Direct reflected light onto a white wall. A band of VIBGYOR colours appears,
proving sunlight contains all seven colours. The water acts as a refracting medium
that separates the colours (dispersion).

Proof 2 -- Glass Prism:
When white sunlight passes through a triangular glass prism, it splits into seven
colours on the other side. Each colour bends by a different amount (violet the most,
red the least) and emerges at a slightly different angle, producing the VIBGYOR spectrum.

Rainbow -- Connection to Sunlight:
A rainbow is a natural dispersion phenomenon seen after rain when sunlight is present.
Millions of tiny water droplets in the atmosphere act as tiny prisms. Sunlight enters
each droplet, undergoes refraction, total internal reflection inside, and refraction
again on exit. Different colours emerge at different angles. The combined effect of
millions of droplets creates the beautiful arc of seven colours (VIBGYOR) in the sky.
This natural phenomenon conclusively proves that sunlight (white light) consists of
seven colours -- which separate when forced to travel through a medium (water droplets).

items.question: White light (sunlight) consists of --
items.explanation: White light consists of seven colours: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red (VIBGYOR).

items.question: The splitting of white light into its constituent colours is called --
items.explanation: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into seven constituent colours when passing through a prism.

items.question: VIBGYOR stands for --

options.A: The seven planets of the solar system
options.B: The seven colours of white light

items.explanation: VIBGYOR is the memory aid for the seven colours of white light in order: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red.

items.question: In the mirror-in-water dispersion activity, the mirror and water together act as --
items.explanation: The water surface and mirror together refract (bend) the different colours of sunlight by different amounts, just like a prism, causing dispersion.

items.question: A rainbow is a natural example of --

options.B: dispersion of sunlight by water droplets

items.explanation: After rain, water droplets in the sky act as tiny prisms. They disperse sunlight into seven colours, forming a rainbow -- a natural dispersion event.

items.question: During dispersion of white light through a prism, which colour bends the most?
items.explanation: During dispersion, violet light bends the most (highest refraction) and red light bends the least. This causes the colours to separate into the spectrum.

items.question: Which colour of light travels at the same speed through a vacuum but bends differently in a glass prism?

options.A: All colours travel at different speeds in vacuum and bend the same in glass
options.B: All colours travel at the same speed in vacuum but bend differently in glass
options.C: Only red and violet travel at the same speed; others differ
options.D: No difference exists; all colours behave identically in all media

items.explanation: In vacuum (or air), all colours of light travel at the same speed (speed of light = 3 x 10^8 m/s). In a denser medium like glass, they slow down by different amounts (violet slows most, red least), causing them to bend (refract) by different amounts -- this is dispersion.

items.question: If you mix the seven colours of the spectrum together, what do you get?
items.explanation: White light is a mixture of all seven colours of VIBGYOR. When the seven spectral colours are mixed in the right proportions, they combine to form white light again. This is why sunlight (white) splits into seven colours and can be recombined.

items.question: In a rainbow, which colour appears at the top of the arc and which at the bottom?

options.A: Violet at top, Red at bottom
options.B: Red at top, Violet at bottom
options.C: Green in the middle, other colours absent at extremes

items.explanation: In a primary rainbow, red appears at the outer (top) arc and violet at the inner (bottom) arc. This is because red bends less (appears at larger angle from the anti-solar point) and violet bends more.

items.question: You are asked to demonstrate that sunlight consists of colours but you have no glass prism. Which simple activity can prove this?

options.A: Shine a torch through a comb onto a mirror
options.B: Place a plane mirror in a bowl of water in sunlight and observe the reflected light
options.C: Look at the Sun directly with the naked eye
options.D: Use a kaleidoscope with coloured glass

items.explanation: The mirror-in-water activity (Activity 13.7) uses water as a refracting medium. Sunlight reflected by the mirror passes through the water layer, causing dispersion. The reflected light shows VIBGYOR colours on a white wall, proving sunlight consists of seven colours.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
The human eye is a roughly spherical sense organ that detects light and enables
vision. It contains several specialised structures: cornea, iris, pupil, lens,
retina, and optic nerve.

sections.label: KEY POINTS (PARTS OF THE EYE):
points: CORNEA: Transparent front part of the eye. Protects the interior from accidents.
It is tough and white (the white outer coat) but its front transparent part is the cornea.
IRIS: Dark muscular structure behind the cornea. Gives the eye its distinctive colour
(brown, blue, green, etc.). Controls the amount of light entering the eye.
PUPIL: Small opening in the centre of the iris through which light enters the eye.
Its size is controlled by the iris.
In DIM LIGHT: pupil becomes LARGER (dilates) to allow more light.
In BRIGHT LIGHT: pupil becomes SMALLER (constricts) to allow less light.
LENS: A convex (thicker at centre) lens behind the pupil. Focuses light on the retina.
The ciliary muscles control the shape/curvature of the lens.
RETINA: Layer at the back of the eye containing light-sensitive nerve cells.
Contains two types of cells:
(i) CONES: Sensitive to bright light; sense colour.
(ii) RODS: Sensitive to dim light; sense intensity (not colour).
OPTIC NERVE: Carries sensations (nerve signals) from the retina to the brain.
BLIND SPOT: The point where the optic nerve meets the retina has NO sensory cells
(no rods or cones). An image formed at this point is NOT seen. Called blind spot.
CILIARY MUSCLE: Muscles attached to the lens; change the curvature of the lens to
focus objects at different distances.
PERSISTENCE OF VISION: An image on the retina persists for about 1/16th of a second
after the light stimulus stops. Moving pictures (movies) use this -- 24 frames per
second gives the illusion of motion.
NIGHT VISION: Night birds (owls) have more RODS and fewer cones -- can see in dim light.
Day birds (eagles, kites) have more CONES and fewer rods -- see well in bright light.
CATARACT: The eye lens becomes cloudy (opaque) with age. Causes loss of vision.
Treated by removing the opaque lens and inserting an artificial lens.
NORMAL VISION DISTANCE: The minimum comfortable reading distance for a normal eye
is about 25 cm (25 centimetres).
ACTIVITY 13.8: Observing the Pupil
AIM: To observe the change in pupil size in dim and bright light.
MATERIALS: A friend, torch.
CAUTION: For this activity, NEVER use a laser torch.
PROCEDURE:
1. Look into your friend's eye. Note the size of the pupil.
2. Throw light on her eye with a torch. Observe the pupil now.
3. Switch off the torch. Observe the pupil again.
OBSERVATION:
In dim light (torch off): Pupil is LARGER.
In bright light (torch on): Pupil becomes SMALLER.
CONCLUSION: The iris controls the size of the pupil. More light -- pupil constricts
(smaller). Less light -- pupil dilates (larger). This controls the amount of light
entering the eye to protect the retina.
ACTIVITY 13.9: Demonstrating the Blind Spot
AIM: To demonstrate the existence of the blind spot in the human eye.
MATERIALS: A sheet of paper with a round mark (dot) and a cross mark (X) drawn on it.
PROCEDURE:
1. On a sheet of paper, make a round mark (dot) and a cross (X) about 6-8 cm apart
(the cross to the right of the dot when held for the left eye test).
2. Hold the paper at arm's length. Close your right eye.
3. Look continuously at the cross with your left eye.
4. Slowly move the sheet toward you, keeping the left eye on the cross.
5. At some point, the round dot will DISAPPEAR.
6. Repeat with the right eye closed: close the left eye, look at the round mark,
move the sheet slowly -- the cross (X) will disappear.
OBSERVATION: At a certain distance, either the dot or the cross disappears from
view even though the eye is open.
CONCLUSION: The disappearance shows that at one specific point on the retina,
there are NO sensory cells (no rods or cones). When the image of the dot/cross
falls on this point, it cannot be seen. This point is called the BLIND SPOT.
It is located at the junction of the optic nerve and the retina.
ACTIVITY 13.10: Persistence of Vision -- Bird in the Cage
AIM: To demonstrate persistence of vision.
MATERIALS: A square piece of cardboard (6-8 cm), string.
PROCEDURE:
1. Make two holes in the cardboard as shown in Fig. 13.16.
2. Draw/paste a cage on one side and a bird on the other side.
3. Thread a string through the two holes.
4. Twist the string and make the card twirl rapidly.
OBSERVATION: You see the bird inside the cage.
CONCLUSION: The eye retains an image for about 1/16th of a second after the light
stops (persistence of vision). When the card spins fast (more than 16 times per
second), both images (bird and cage) persist on the retina simultaneously, creating
the illusion of the bird being inside the cage. Movies use this principle --
24 frames/second gives the illusion of motion.
DIAGRAM:
[Fig. 13.14 -- Human eye diagram showing: Ciliary muscle, Iris, Lens, Cornea,
Retina, Optic Nerve -- all labelled]
[Fig. 13.15 -- Blind spot demonstration: cross (X) and dot on paper]
[Fig. 13.16 -- Bird in cage activity: card with cage on one side, bird on other,
string through holes]

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS (DO YOU KNOW? box, p.92):
sections.text:
Animals have eyes of different shapes. Eyes of a crab are quite small but enable
the crab to look all around (see even from behind). Butterflies have large eyes
made up of thousands of little eyes (Fig. 13.17), so they can see in front, sides,
and back simultaneously. A night bird (owl) can see very well at night but not
during the day. It has a large cornea and large pupil to allow more light; large
number of rods on retina (sensitive to dim light) but only a few cones. Day light
birds (kite, eagle) can see well during the day but not at night -- they have more
cones (sensitive to bright light) and fewer rods.

items.question: What is the function of the iris in the human eye?
items.answer:
The iris is a dark muscular structure behind the cornea. It gives the eye its
distinctive colour and controls the amount of light entering the eye by changing
the size of the pupil.

items.question: What is the blind spot in the human eye?
items.answer:
The blind spot is the point on the retina where the optic nerve is attached.
At this point, there are no sensory cells (no rods or cones). An object whose
image falls on the blind spot cannot be seen.

items.question: What are the functions of rods and cones in the human eye?
items.answer:
RODS:
- Located on the retina.
- Sensitive to dim light.
- Help us see in low light conditions.
- Cannot distinguish colours.
- Night birds (owls) have more rods than cones.
CONES:
- Located on the retina.
- Sensitive to bright light.
- Help us detect colours.
- Day birds (eagles) have more cones than rods.
Together, rods and cones convert light into nerve signals that the optic nerve
carries to the brain.

items.answer:

- IRIS: Coloured muscular ring controlling pupil size
- PUPIL: Dark opening in the centre of iris for light entry
- LENS: Convex lens focusing light on retina
- CILIARY MUSCLE: Controls lens curvature for focusing
- RETINA: Rear layer of the eye with rods and cones
- OPTIC NERVE: Carries signals from retina to brain
