items.question: How does the pupil change in dim and bright light? Describe an
items.answer:
Pupil Size Change:
- In BRIGHT LIGHT: Pupil becomes SMALLER (contracts/constricts).
- In DIM LIGHT: Pupil becomes LARGER (dilates).

sections.label: Activity 13.8:
procedure: Observe friend's pupil size in normal light. Shine torch on the eye
-- pupil immediately contracts. Switch off torch -- pupil dilates (becomes larger).
Reason: The pupil controls the amount of light entering the eye. In bright light,
too much light would damage the retina, so the iris constricts the pupil to reduce
light entry. In dim light, the pupil dilates to allow more light in for better vision.
Q6 [4 Marks]: What is persistence of vision? How do movies make use of this?
A6: PERSISTENCE OF VISION: After the stimulus (light) stops falling on the retina,
the impression of the image remains on the retina for about 1/16th of a second.
This phenomenon is called persistence of vision.
Demonstration (Activity 13.10): A card with a bird on one side and a cage on the
other is spun rapidly using a twisted string. When the card spins faster than 16
times per second, both images (bird and cage) persist on the retina simultaneously.
The brain perceives both at once, creating the illusion that the bird is inside the cage.
Application in Movies: A motion picture is actually a series of still photographs
(frames) shown rapidly. Modern cinema shows 24 frames per second. Since each frame
persists on the retina for 1/16th of a second (longer than the interval between frames),
the viewer sees continuous motion rather than separate still images. This is the
basis of motion pictures (cinema).
Q7 [6 Marks]: Describe the structure of the human eye and explain how it enables us
to see. Include the roles of all major parts: cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina,
rods, cones, optic nerve, and blind spot.
Structure of the Human Eye:
The eye is roughly spherical in shape. It is surrounded by a tough white outer coat
that protects the interior. The front transparent part is the CORNEA.
Parts and Their Functions:
1. CORNEA: Transparent front cover. Allows light to enter. First refraction of light
occurs here. Protects the eye from accidents.
2. IRIS: Dark muscular ring behind cornea. Gives eye its colour. Controls size of pupil.
3. PUPIL: Small opening in the centre of iris. Allows light to enter the lens.
Size controlled by iris: large in dim light (more light), small in bright light (less light).
4. LENS: Convex lens made of transparent material. Focuses light precisely on the retina.
Ciliary muscles adjust its curvature for near and far objects (accommodation).
5. RETINA: Rear layer of the eye. Contains two types of light-sensitive cells:
- RODS: Sensitive to dim light; cannot detect colour.
- CONES: Sensitive to bright light; detect colour.
The retina converts light energy into nerve signals.
6. OPTIC NERVE: Carries nerve signals from retina to the brain. The brain interprets
these signals as visual images.
7. BLIND SPOT: The junction of optic nerve and retina has no rods or cones.
Images falling here cannot be seen.
8. CILIARY MUSCLE: Attached to the lens; changes lens curvature to focus objects
at varying distances.
How Vision Occurs:
Light from an object enters through the cornea, passes through the pupil, is focused
by the lens, and falls on the retina. Rods and cones convert light to electrical
signals. Optic nerve carries signals to brain. Brain interprets signals -- we "see" the object.

items.question: The part of the eye that controls the amount of light entering is --
items.explanation: The iris is a muscular structure that controls the size of the pupil, thereby controlling how much light enters the eye.

items.question: The retina of the eye contains --
items.explanation: The retina contains both rods (sensitive to dim light, detect intensity) and cones (sensitive to bright light, detect colour).

items.question: The blind spot in the eye is the point where --

options.B: the optic nerve is attached to the retina

items.explanation: The blind spot is the junction of the optic nerve and the retina, where there are no rods or cones. Images formed here cannot be sensed.

items.question: The size of the pupil becomes larger when --
items.explanation: In dim light, the iris expands the pupil (dilates) to allow more light to enter the eye for better vision in low-light conditions.

items.question: Night birds like owls can see in the dark because they have --

options.C: equal numbers of rods and cones

items.explanation: Rods are sensitive to dim light. Owls have more rods, enabling them to see well in low light (at night). Cones (sensitive to bright light) are fewer.

items.question: Cataract is a condition where --
items.explanation: In cataract, the eye lens becomes opaque (cloudy). Light cannot pass through clearly, causing vision loss. It is treated by replacing the lens.

items.question: The minimum distance at which a normal human eye can see objects most comfortably is --
items.explanation: The minimum comfortable reading/viewing distance for a normal eye is about 25 cm. Closer than this, the ciliary muscles strain to focus the lens.

items.question: An image persists on the retina for --
items.explanation: The impression of an image persists on the retina for about 1/16th of a second after the light source is removed. This is called persistence of vision.

items.question: Movies give the illusion of motion because --

options.B: 24 still frames per second are shown, and persistence of vision causes us
options.D: the sound track creates the illusion of movement

items.explanation: Movies consist of 24 still frames per second. Due to persistence of vision (1/16th of a second), each frame still persists when the next frame appears, giving the brain a continuous visual signal that it perceives as motion.

items.question: Day birds like eagles have more cones than rods. This means they can --

options.A: see well in dim light but not in bright light
options.B: see colour clearly in bright light but not in dim light
options.C: see equally well in all light conditions

items.explanation: Cones are sensitive to bright light and detect colour. More cones means better colour vision in bright daylight. Since they have fewer rods, vision in dim or dark conditions is poor.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
Care of the eyes refers to the practices and precautions that protect the eyes
from injury, strain and disease, ensuring good vision throughout life.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Eyes are our most important sense organs for vision -- they need proper care.
EYE SPECIALIST: If any problem occurs with vision or the eyes, visit an ophthalmologist.
REGULAR CHECK-UP: Have regular eye examinations.
SPECTACLES: If advised by a doctor, wear appropriate corrective spectacles.
LIGHT: Too little light causes eye strain and headaches. Too much light (e.g., bright
sunlight or laser) can injure the retina.
DIRECT SUNLIGHT: Never look at the Sun directly or at a powerful light source.
DUST IN EYES: Never rub eyes if dust enters. Wash with clean water.
READING DISTANCE: Always read at the normal/comfortable distance (about 25 cm).
Do not bring books too close or keep them too far.
VITAMIN A: Eye deficiency in Vitamin A leads to NIGHT BLINDNESS (cannot see in dim light).
Include Vitamin A rich foods: raw carrots, broccoli, green vegetables (spinach),
cod liver oil, eggs, milk, curd, cheese, butter, papaya, mango.
LASER TORCH: Never use a laser torch to observe the pupil or direct it toward eyes.
Laser light can permanently damage the retina.
EYE DONATION: Eyes can be donated after death to help blind persons (corneal blindness).
Eyes must be donated within 4-6 hours after death.

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS (DID YOU KNOW? box, p.98):
sections.text:
Eyes can be donated by any person suffering from corneal blindness after death.
Donor may be: male or female, any age, any social status, spectacle wearers.
Exception: persons with AIDS, Hepatitis B or C, rabies, leukemia, lymphoma,
tetanus, cholera, encephalitis cannot donate eyes.
Eyes must be donated within 4-6 hours of death, at any place (home or hospital).
Anyone wishing to donate eyes should pledge at a registered eye bank and inform
relatives so they can act after death. You can also donate a Braille kit.

EXERCISE 13.8.1: Gurmit wanted to perform Activity 13.8 using a laser torch.
Her teacher advised her not to do so. Can you explain the basis of the teacher's advice?
EXERCISE ANSWER: A laser torch produces a very intense and concentrated beam of light.
If this falls on the retina of the eye, it can cause permanent damage or even
blindness. That is why the teacher advised against using a laser torch for
observing pupil changes.

EXERCISE 13.8.2: Explain how you can take care of your eyes.
EXERCISE ANSWER:
- Have regular eye check-ups and use spectacles if advised.
- Do not read in too little or too much light.
- Do not look at the Sun or powerful light directly -- it can injure the retina.
- Never rub your eyes. If particles of dust enter, wash eyes with clean water.
- Always read at the normal distance (about 25 cm); do not bring the book too close.
- Include Vitamin A rich food in diet (carrots, broccoli, spinach, eggs, milk, fruits).

items.question: Name two practices that help take care of your eyes.
items.answer:
Two practices for eye care:
1. Avoid looking directly at the Sun or powerful light sources, as they can damage the retina.
2. Always read at normal distance (about 25 cm) and in adequate light to prevent eyestrain.

items.question: What deficiency causes night blindness? Name two food sources that
items.answer:
Night blindness is caused by deficiency of VITAMIN A in the diet. Food sources
rich in Vitamin A: raw carrots, broccoli, green leafy vegetables (spinach), eggs,
milk, butter (any two).

items.question: List any six precautions for the care of eyes.
items.answer:
Six precautions for eye care:
1. Have regular eye check-ups; wear spectacles if advised.
2. Do not read in too little or too much light (avoid eye strain).
3. Never look at the Sun or powerful light directly (damages retina).
4. Never rub eyes; if dust enters, wash with clean water.
5. Always read at the normal distance (about 25 cm).
6. Include Vitamin A rich food in diet to prevent night blindness
(carrots, spinach, eggs, milk, fruits).

items.question: Why should you not use a laser torch to shine on someone's eye?
items.answer:
A laser torch produces a very concentrated, high-intensity beam of light.
Unlike ordinary torchlight, laser light does not spread out. If directed into the
eye, even briefly, the intense laser beam can cause irreversible damage to the
retina (the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye). This can result in
permanent loss of vision or blindness. Therefore, laser torches must never be
used to shine into eyes. That is why, in Activity 13.8 (pupil observation),
the textbook specifically cautions: "For this activity, never use a laser torch."

items.question: How does Vitamin A deficiency affect vision? What foods can
items.answer:
VITAMIN A DEFICIENCY AND VISION:
Vitamin A is essential for the production of a light-sensitive pigment (rhodopsin)
in the rod cells of the retina. Rod cells are responsible for vision in dim light.
When Vitamin A is deficient:
- Rhodopsin cannot be produced in adequate amounts.
- Rod cells cannot function properly in low light.
- The person cannot see clearly in dim light or at night.
- This condition is called NIGHT BLINDNESS.
Severe Vitamin A deficiency can also cause the cornea to dry out and become
damaged, potentially leading to complete blindness.
Foods rich in Vitamin A (to prevent deficiency):
1. Raw carrots
2. Broccoli
3. Green leafy vegetables (spinach, methi)
4. Cod liver oil
5. Eggs
6. Milk, curd, cheese, butter
7. Yellow and orange fruits: papaya, mango.

items.question: Why should you not look at the Sun directly? What could happen?
items.answer:
Danger of Looking at the Sun Directly:
Sunlight is extremely intense. When you look directly at the Sun, the concentrated
sunlight is focused by the eye's lens onto a tiny spot on the retina. The intense
energy burns the retinal cells permanently. This is called solar retinopathy.
Effects:
- Permanent damage to rods and cones in the area of focus.
- Loss of vision in that area (a dark or blurred spot in vision).
- In severe cases, permanent blindness.
Prevention:
- Never look at the Sun directly with naked eyes.
- Do not look at any bright, powerful light source directly.
- During solar eclipses, use specially designed solar eclipse glasses.
- A laser torch is equally dangerous -- never aim it at any person's eyes.

items.question: Write a detailed note on "Care of the Eyes" including precautions,
items.answer:
CARE OF THE EYES:
Introduction: Eyes are our most important sense organs. Proper care ensures good
vision throughout life. Once damaged, vision loss is often permanent.

Precautions:
1. Regular check-up: Visit an ophthalmologist (eye specialist) regularly for checkups.
Wear spectacles if prescribed.
2. Light: Too little light causes eye strain and headaches. Too much light damages
the retina. Read in adequate, comfortable light.
3. Avoid direct sunlight: Never look at the Sun or a powerful lamp directly.
The intense light can permanently burn the retina, causing blindness.
4. Laser safety: Never use a laser torch near the eyes. Laser light causes instant,
permanent retinal damage.
5. Dust: If particles enter the eye, never rub them. Rubbing can scratch the cornea.
Wash the eye gently with clean water. If no improvement, see a doctor.
6. Reading distance: Always read at about 25 cm (normal comfortable distance).
Do not hold the book too close or too far; both cause strain.

Dietary Measures:
Vitamin A is essential for the function of rod cells (vision in dim light).
Deficiency causes night blindness. Foods rich in Vitamin A: raw carrots, broccoli,
green leafy vegetables, eggs, milk, butter, papaya, mango. Include these regularly.

Eye Donation:
Healthy eyes can be donated after death to help persons with corneal blindness.
Donor can be of any gender, age, or social status. Spectacle wearers can also donate.
Exceptions: persons with AIDS, Hepatitis B/C, rabies, leukemia, lymphoma, tetanus,
cholera, encephalitis.
Eyes must be donated within 4-6 hours of death, at home or hospital.
To participate: pledge at a registered eye bank during lifetime and inform relatives.
Eye donation restores sight and is a noble gift to society. You can also donate a Braille kit.

items.question: Night blindness is caused by deficiency of --
items.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency prevents the production of rhodopsin in rod cells, causing night blindness (inability to see in dim light).

items.question: If dust enters your eye, you should --

options.C: wash the eye with clean water
options.D: use a finger to remove the dust

items.explanation: Rubbing can scratch the cornea or push the dust further in. Washing with clean water is the safe first response. See a doctor if no improvement.

items.question: The comfortable reading distance for a normal eye is about --
items.explanation: The normal comfortable reading distance (least distance of distinct vision) for a normal human eye is approximately 25 cm (25 centimetres).

items.question: Which of the following food items is rich in Vitamin A?
items.explanation: Raw carrots are rich in beta-carotene, which the body converts to Vitamin A. Deficiency of Vitamin A causes night blindness.

items.question: Why should you never use a laser torch to perform the pupil observation activity?

options.A: Laser light is too dim to see the pupil
options.B: Laser light is so intense it can permanently damage the retina
options.C: Laser light does not reflect from the pupil

items.explanation: Laser light is extremely intense and concentrated. Even brief exposure can burn retinal cells permanently, causing irreversible damage to vision.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT a correct eye care practice?

options.C: Rubbing the eye with your hand if dust enters
options.D: Having a Vitamin A rich diet

items.explanation: Rubbing the eye when dust enters is wrong -- it can scratch the cornea or push dust deeper. The correct action is to wash with clean water.

items.question: Eyes donated after death must be used within --
items.explanation: For eye donation to be useful for transplantation, the eyes must be donated (collected) within 4-6 hours after the person's death.

items.question: A person cannot see clearly in dim light but sees well in bright light. He most likely suffers from --
items.explanation: Night blindness is the inability to see in dim light, caused by Vitamin A deficiency leading to defective rod cells. Vision in bright light (cone cells) remains normal.

items.question: Who CANNOT donate eyes after death?

options.B: A 30-year-old man of any social status
options.D: A person who had cataract surgery

items.explanation: Persons with certain infections (AIDS, Hepatitis B/C, rabies, leukemia, lymphoma, tetanus, cholera, encephalitis) cannot donate eyes due to risk of transmitting disease. Age, gender, social status, and spectacle use are not barriers to eye donation.

items.question: What is the consequence of severe, untreated Vitamin A deficiency beyond night blindness?

options.B: The cornea dries out and gets damaged, potentially causing complete blindness

items.explanation: Prolonged, severe Vitamin A deficiency causes Xerophthalmia -- the cornea dries, becomes ulcerated and damaged. If untreated, this leads to permanent corneal scarring and complete blindness, not just night blindness.

topics.topic_name: VISUALLY IMPAIRED PERSONS CAN READ AND WRITE

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
Visually impaired persons are those with very limited or no vision. Special
resources -- optical aids, non-optical aids and the Braille system -- help them
to read, write and function in daily life.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Some persons are visually impaired (very limited vision) or blind (no vision at all).
Causes: born with limited vision, or lost sight due to disease or injury.
Visually impaired persons rely more on their sense of TOUCH and HEARING.
They develop other senses more sharply.
SPECIAL RESOURCES available:
1. NON-OPTICAL AIDS: Visual aids (magnify without lens), tactual aids (sense of touch),
auditory aids (sense of hearing), electronic aids.
TACTUAL AIDS: Braille writer slate and stylus -- help in taking notes, reading, writing.
AUDITORY AIDS: Cassettes, tape recorders, talking books, etc.
ELECTRONIC AIDS: Talking calculators, computers, closed circuit televisions,
voice boxes, audio CDs.
2. OPTICAL AIDS: Bifocal lenses, contact lenses, tinted lenses, magnifiers,
telescopic aids (for seeing chalkboard/demonstrations from a distance).
The most well-known resource for visually impaired persons is BRAILLE.

items.question: Who are visually impaired persons?
items.answer:
Persons with very limited vision or no vision at all are called visually impaired.
Some are born visually impaired; others lose their sight due to disease or injury.
They have very limited ability or no ability to see things.

items.question: Name any two non-optical aids available for visually impaired persons.
items.answer:
Two non-optical aids:
1. TACTUAL AIDS: Braille writer slate and stylus for reading and writing by touch.
2. AUDITORY AIDS: Cassettes, tape recorders, talking books for learning by hearing.

items.question: What are optical aids for visually impaired persons? Name any four.
items.answer:
Optical aids use lenses or optical instruments to enhance limited vision.
Four optical aids for visually impaired:
1. Bifocal lenses: Correct both near and far vision in one lens.
2. Contact lenses: Placed directly on the cornea for correction.
3. Tinted lenses (special sunglasses): Reduce glare and improve contrast.
4. Telescopic aids: Help see distant objects like a chalkboard or classroom demonstrations.
(Also: magnifiers for reading close text.)

items.question: How do visually impaired persons develop their other senses?
items.answer:
Visually impaired persons, unable to rely on sight, compensate by developing
other senses more sharply:
1. SENSE OF TOUCH: They learn to identify objects, read Braille, and navigate
by feeling surfaces, textures and raised patterns.
2. SENSE OF HEARING: They listen carefully to voices, footsteps, sounds of traffic
and other environmental sounds to understand their surroundings.
3. SENSE OF SMELL: Some develop this sense further for identifying people and places.
4. SPATIAL MEMORY: They memorise the layout of familiar environments to move confidently.
These developed abilities allow visually impaired persons to lead independent and
productive lives.

items.question: Describe any three electronic aids available for visually impaired persons.
items.answer:
Three electronic aids for visually impaired:
1. TALKING CALCULATORS: Calculators that speak out numbers, operations and results aloud.
Visually impaired persons can perform calculations without seeing the display.
2. COMPUTERS WITH VOICE BOXES (Screen Readers): Computers fitted with software that
reads out text displayed on the screen. Allows visually impaired persons to read
documents, emails and web pages by listening.
3. CLOSED CIRCUIT TELEVISION (CCTV): An electronic aid that magnifies and enhances
printed material with suitable contrast and illumination on a screen. Helps persons
with limited vision read printed text.
(Also available: Audio CDs, talking books, voice recorders.)

items.question: What kind of special resources do visually impaired persons need?
items.answer:
Special Resources for Visually Impaired:
1. NON-OPTICAL AIDS:
a. Visual aids: Magnify words without a lens system; provide proper distance and illumination.
b. Tactual aids: Use sense of touch (e.g., Braille writer slate and stylus, raised maps).
c. Auditory aids: Use sense of hearing (e.g., talking books, tape recorders, cassettes).
d. Electronic aids: Use technology (e.g., talking calculators, CCTV, computers with voice boxes).
2. OPTICAL AIDS:
a. Bifocal lenses and contact lenses: Correct vision for limited-sight persons.
b. Magnifiers and telescopic aids: Enlarge text and distant objects to be visible.
These resources allow visually impaired persons to study, work, and participate in daily life.

items.question: Describe the challenges faced by visually impaired persons and explain
items.answer:
Challenges Faced by Visually Impaired Persons:
1. Cannot read printed text without special aids.
2. Cannot see faces, expressions, or surroundings.
3. Difficulty navigating unfamiliar environments.
4. Limited access to standard educational materials.
5. Dependence on others for many activities.

How Special Resources Help:
1. Braille system (tactual): Allows reading and writing by touch. Available for languages
(including Indian languages), mathematics, scientific notation, music.
2. Talking books and audio CDs (auditory): Allow listening to educational content.
3. Telescopic aids (optical): Help see chalkboard and classroom demonstrations from a distance.
4. Computers with voice boxes / CCTV (electronic): Enable word processing, internet browsing
and reading documents independently.
5. Tactual aids (Braille slate and stylus): Allow taking notes during lessons.

Inspiring Real-Life Examples:
1. DIWAKAR (Indian): A visually impaired child prodigy -- gave amazing performances as a singer.
2. RAVINDRA JAIN: Born completely visually impaired; obtained Sangeet Prabhakar degree from
Allahabad. Achieved excellence as a lyricist, singer and music composer.
3. LAL ADVANI: Visually impaired; established an Association for special education and
rehabilitation of disabled in India. Represented India on Braille problems at UNESCO.
4. HELEN A. KELLER (American): Lost sight at 18 months old. Because of her resolve and courage,
she completed graduation from a university and wrote many books including "The Story of
My Life" (1903). One of the most inspiring visually impaired persons in the world.

Conclusion: With the right resources and support, visually impaired persons can
achieve great things in education, arts, science and public life.

items.question: Visually impaired persons rely more on which senses?
items.explanation: Visually impaired persons develop their sense of touch (to read Braille, feel surroundings) and hearing (to listen to talking books, sounds of environment) more sharply to compensate for limited or no vision.

items.question: Which of the following is a tactual aid for visually impaired persons?
items.explanation: A Braille writer slate and stylus is a tactual aid -- it uses the sense of touch for writing and reading in Braille. Telescope and contact lens are optical aids; CCTV is an electronic aid.

items.question: Helen A. Keller became visually impaired at the age of --
items.explanation: Helen A. Keller lost her sight when she was only 18 months old. Despite this, she completed university education and wrote many books.

items.question: A telescopic aid is classified as which type of aid?
items.explanation: Telescopic aids use optical lenses to magnify distant objects (like a chalkboard) and are classified as optical aids.

items.question: Which of the following is an electronic aid for visually impaired persons?
items.explanation: A talking calculator is an electronic aid that speaks out numbers and results. Braille slate is tactual; magnifier is optical; contact lens is optical.

items.question: Auditory aids for the visually impaired include --

options.C: Talking books, tape recorders and cassettes

items.explanation: Auditory aids use the sense of hearing: talking books, tape recorders, cassettes. Bifocal lenses and magnifiers are optical; Braille slates are tactual; CCTV and computers are electronic aids.

items.question: Which Indian visually impaired person represented India on Braille problems at UNESCO?
items.explanation: Lal Advani, himself visually impaired, established an Association for special education and rehabilitation of disabled persons in India and represented India on Braille problems at UNESCO.

items.question: A closed circuit television (CCTV) helps visually impaired persons by --

options.A: converting text to audio so they can hear it
options.B: enlarging and enhancing printed material with suitable contrast and illumination
options.C: producing Braille output directly from books
options.D: transmitting images to the visual cortex of the brain

items.explanation: CCTV enlarges printed material on a screen with suitable contrast and illumination, helping persons with limited (but not zero) vision to read.

items.question: Why do visually impaired persons often develop a sharper sense of touch and hearing?

options.A: Their brain automatically compensates by growing more nerve cells
options.B: Without visual input, they consciously and habitually use other senses more,
options.C: Blindness chemically enhances the ears and skin
options.D: They receive special injections that enhance other senses

items.explanation: The brain is adaptable (neuroplasticity). When vision is absent, more of the brain's processing power is devoted to touch and hearing. Regular, intensive use of these senses strengthens the neural connections, making them sharper over time.

items.question: Ravindra Jain, who was born completely visually impaired, achieved excellence as a --
items.explanation: Ravindra Jain, born completely visually impaired, obtained the Sangeet Prabhakar degree from Allahabad and achieved excellence as a lyricist, singer and music composer -- a remarkable achievement.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
The Braille system is a tactile reading and writing system for visually impaired
persons, based on raised dot patterns that can be felt by fingertips. It was
developed by Louis Braille in 1821 and officially adopted in 1932.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: DEVELOPER: Louis Braille -- himself a visually challenged person; developed the system
in 1821; published it. The system was officially adopted worldwide in 1932.
PRINCIPLE: Characters are represented by raised dot patterns arranged in cells of
two vertical rows of three dots each (2 columns x 3 rows = 6 dots per cell).
CHARACTERS: 63 dot patterns (characters) are possible (2^6 - 1 = 63 patterns,
excluding the blank cell). The textbook states 63 dot patterns or characters.
EACH CHARACTER represents: a letter, a combination of letters, a common word,
or a grammatical sign.
READING METHOD: Fingertips move across the raised dots to recognise patterns.
LEARNING: Braille is learned by starting with letters, then special characters
and letter combinations. Each character must be memorised.
LANGUAGES: Braille code exists for common languages, mathematics and scientific notation.
Many Indian languages can be read using Braille system.
WRITING: Braille texts can be produced by hand (using Braille slate and stylus)
or by machine (typewriter-like Braille writers and Braille printing machines).
The present Braille system was adopted in 1932.
BRAILLE DOT CELL STRUCTURE:
Each character is formed in a cell of 2 columns x 3 rows = 6 dots.
Dots that are raised represent the character; dots not raised leave blank spaces.
Example from textbook (Fig. 13.18):
C = two raised dots in column 1 (top two dots raised, column 2 blank)
A = one raised dot (top of column 1 only)
T = raised dots forming a different pattern (top right and middle right)
C + A + T = CAT
METHODS OF PRODUCING BRAILLE TEXT:
1. BY HAND: Braille writer slate + stylus (punch dots into thick paper/Braille paper).
2. BY MACHINE: Typewriter-like Braille writers (faster, more regular dots).
3. BY PRINTING MACHINE: Mass production of Braille books and materials.
INSPIRING EXAMPLE:
Louis Braille (shown in Fig. 13.18) -- a French visually impaired person who
developed this system. He could not see from childhood due to an accident.
DIAGRAM:

Showing the dot patterns for C, A, T forming CAT, and pattern for 'and' and comma (,)]

items.question: Who invented the Braille system and when?
items.answer:
The Braille system was invented by Louis Braille, himself a visually challenged
person. He developed and published it in 1821. The present system was officially
adopted worldwide in 1932.

items.question: How many dot patterns does the Braille system have?
items.answer:
The Braille system has 63 dot patterns or characters. Each cell consists of
two vertical rows of three dots each (6 dot positions), allowing 63 different
raised dot patterns (excluding the blank cell).

items.question: Describe the structure of a Braille character cell. How does it work?
items.answer:
Structure of a Braille Character Cell:
- Each character in Braille is contained in a cell.
- The cell has 2 columns and 3 rows -- totalling 6 dot positions.
- Some dot positions have RAISED dots (felt by touch); others are blank (not raised).
- The specific pattern of raised and blank dots in the 6 positions represents a
particular letter, word, combination of letters or grammatical sign.
How it works: The reader places fingertips on the Braille sheet and moves them
from left to right. The fingertips feel the raised dots and identify the pattern,
which the brain recognises as the corresponding letter, word or symbol.

items.question: What does each Braille character represent? How is Braille read?
items.answer:
Each Braille character (dot pattern) can represent:
- A letter of the alphabet (e.g., C, A, T)
- A common word
- A combination of letters
- A grammatical sign (e.g., comma, period)
How Braille is Read:
Braille readers begin by learning individual letter patterns, then letter combinations
and special characters. Reading is done by touch -- fingertips move across the page,
left to right, line by line. Each raised dot pattern is felt and instantly recognised
as a letter, word or sign. With practice, skilled Braille readers can read at
considerable speed. Each character must be separately memorised through practice.

items.question: How can Braille text be produced? Describe the methods.
items.answer:
Braille text can be produced by three methods:
Method 1 -- By Hand (Braille Slate and Stylus):
A Braille slate is a metal guide with cells. A stylus is a pointed tool. The writer
places thick Braille paper on the slate and uses the stylus to punch raised dots in
the cell positions. This is done from right to left (since the dots are read from
the front, which is the reverse side). Producing text by hand is slower but portable.
Method 2 -- Braille Typewriter:
A typewriter-like device with 6 keys (one for each dot position) and a space bar.
The writer presses combinations of keys to produce raised dot patterns on Braille paper.
Faster and more regular than hand punching.
Method 3 -- Braille Printing Machine:
For mass production of Braille books and materials. A printing machine embosses
(raises) dot patterns on Braille paper in bulk. Used for publishing Braille textbooks,
newspapers and other reading material at scale.

items.question: Who was Louis Braille? Write a short note on his contribution
items.answer:
LOUIS BRAILLE (1809-1852):
Louis Braille was a French visually impaired person who developed the Braille system.
He lost his sight as a young child due to an accident while playing with his father's
tools. He later became a student at the National Institute for the Blind in Paris.
Contribution:
1. Braille invented a system of raised dot patterns in 1821 that allowed visually
impaired persons to read and write by touch.
2. The system has 63 characters (dot patterns in 2x3 cells), each representing a
letter, word, or grammatical sign.
3. Braille code now exists for most languages worldwide, including many Indian languages,
as well as mathematics and scientific notation.
4. The system was officially adopted internationally in 1932 and remains the primary
literacy system for visually impaired persons globally.
Impact: Braille's invention transformed the lives of millions of visually impaired
persons worldwide, giving them access to education, literature and written communication
that was previously impossible. It is one of the most significant humanitarian inventions.

items.question: Describe the Braille system in detail -- its invention, structure,
items.answer:
Invention:
The Braille system was invented by Louis Braille, a French visually challenged person,
in 1821. Louis Braille lost his sight in childhood and experienced firsthand the
difficulty of reading without vision. He developed a system of raised dots that could
be felt by the fingertips. The current system was officially adopted worldwide in 1932.

Structure:
Each Braille character is formed in a cell of 2 columns and 3 rows (6 dot positions).
Any of the 6 positions may be raised (dot present) or flat (no dot). This gives 2^6 - 1
= 63 possible patterns (excluding the all-blank cell). The Braille system uses all 63
patterns as characters representing letters, words, and symbols.

How It Works:
- The reader moves fingertips across the page from left to right, line by line.
- Each cell's raised dot pattern is felt and recognised as a letter, word, or sign.
- Example: C is represented by two raised dots (top two of left column); A by one
raised dot (top of left column); T by a different pattern.
- Words can be represented character by character or by special single-character
shorthand for common words (contracted Braille).

How Braille Text is Produced:
1. By hand: Braille slate and stylus -- punch dots into thick paper from right to left.
2. By Braille typewriter: Six-key device that embosses dots simultaneously, faster.
3. By Braille printing machine: For mass production of Braille books.

Languages Using Braille:
Braille code exists for all major languages worldwide. Many Indian languages can be
written in Braille. Braille is also available for mathematics and scientific notation,
and even for musical notation. This universal adaptability makes it the primary tool
for literacy for visually impaired persons globally.

Significance:
Before Braille, visually impaired persons had very limited access to written knowledge.
The Braille system gave them independence, access to education, and the ability to
participate fully in society. It remains in wide use today alongside modern electronic aids.

items.question: The Braille system was developed by --
items.explanation: Louis Braille, a visually challenged French person, developed the Braille system in 1821. Helen A. Keller was a famous blind person but did not develop the Braille system.

items.question: The Braille system uses --
items.explanation: Braille uses raised dot patterns in cells that can be felt by the fingertips. It does not use visual symbols, colours or large print.

items.question: The number of dot patterns in the Braille system is --
items.explanation: The Braille system has 63 dot patterns or characters, formed by different combinations of raised dots in a 2x3 cell (6 positions: 2^6 - 1 = 63).

items.question: Each Braille cell consists of --
items.explanation: Each Braille cell has 2 vertical columns, each with 3 dots, giving 6 dot positions per cell. Different combinations of raised dots in these 6 positions form the 63 Braille characters.

items.question: Braille was officially adopted worldwide in --
items.explanation: Louis Braille developed and published the system in 1821, but the present Braille system was officially adopted internationally in 1932.

items.question: In the Braille system, each character can represent --

options.B: A letter, a combination of letters, a common word or a grammatical sign

items.explanation: Each Braille character (dot pattern) can represent a letter, a combination of letters, a common word, or a grammatical sign (like a comma). This makes the system versatile and efficient.

items.question: Braille text can be produced by which of the following methods?

options.A: Only by hand using a slate and stylus
options.B: By hand (slate/stylus), by Braille typewriter, or by Braille printing machine
options.D: By embroidering raised patterns on cloth

items.explanation: Braille can be produced by three methods: (1) hand-punching with a Braille slate and stylus, (2) a Braille typewriter (6-key device), and (3) a Braille printing machine for mass production.

items.question: Which of the following correctly describes why the Braille system has 63 characters?

options.A: 63 is the number of letters in all languages combined
options.B: A cell with 6 dot positions gives 2^6 - 1 = 63 possible non-blank combinations
options.D: 63 matches the number of sounds in French language

items.explanation: With 6 dot positions in each cell, each position can be raised or not (2 choices). Total combinations = 2^6 = 64. Excluding the blank cell (all not raised), there are 64 - 1 = 63 meaningful patterns.

items.question: Why does learning Braille require each character to be memorised separately?

options.A: Because Braille uses no consistent pattern -- each character is arbitrary
options.B: Because there is no visual cue (you cannot see the dots while reading) --
options.C: Because Braille changes from country to country
options.D: Because Braille is not related to any existing alphabet

items.explanation: Unlike sighted reading where you see and recognise shapes visually, Braille reading requires the fingertips to feel the dot pattern and the brain to match it to a memorised association. Without visual reinforcement, each pattern must be committed to tactile memory through practice.

items.question: Braille code is available for which of the following?

options.C: Common languages, mathematics and scientific notation, including many Indian languages
options.D: Only mathematics; language text uses a different system

items.explanation: Braille is available for most world languages including many Indian languages. It also has codes for mathematics and scientific notation, and even musical notation, making it a comprehensive literacy system for visually impaired persons.
